Loop Engineering + Jev Engineering: Cut Your Claude Bill

A Claude automation can spend tokens checking an empty queue, rereading an unchanged issue, or deciding whether to try again.
Put those decisions on their own path, and you can control exactly what starts a run and what keeps it alive.
Jev gives that path a useful building block: typed answers that your code can route. Claude handles the implementation, while your application controls which tasks reach it.
Start with one recurring workflow. By the end, you will have a small issue filter you can run, a way to evaluate its mistakes, and a design for extending it to tool checks and completion checks.

Find the decisions you keep paying for
Take a recent automated run and look at the questions between productive actions. A queue watcher might repeatedly ask whether a new report contains enough information to investigate.
Useful candidates include:
Classifying an incoming issue.
Selecting a handler from a fixed list.
Checking whether an output addresses a written requirement.
Deciding whether new evidence warrants another agent run.
Write down each question, how often it appears, and what information answers it.
That inventory gives you a concrete starting point for loop engineering.
Anthropic already recommends moving suitable processing into hooks and keeping verbose operations out of the main conversation.

For an issue watcher, first check whether anything changed using identifiers and timestamps.
When the queue is unchanged, ordinary code can end the check immediately.
A new issue then reaches a semantic filter. Only an accepted task proceeds to the coding agent, with the relevant report and a specific requested outcome.
That order matters because a classifier also consumes resources.
Apply it to decisions that require reading meaning; keep exact comparisons and counters in code.

What Jev actually returns
Jev is TypeSafe AI's decision model.
You send a state, such as an issue report, alongside questions with defined answer formats.

The three question types cover different jobs:
Choice returns the selected option and a probability distribution; Noul returns the probability of yes. Score returns a value across your ordered levels.

The current documented model, jev-1.13.0, costs $0.042 per million input tokens, with output tokens free.

Build a filter you can inspect
Use Python 3 in a local working folder. Install the official package. Create an API key and set TYPESAFE_API_KEY. Save a sample issue.json and triage.py that prints a proposed route without launching Claude.

Make confidence useful in your workflow
The 0.9 thresholds are initial settings. Choose production thresholds from labeled examples. Run in shadow mode first.

Connect accepted reports to a bounded Claude run
Store accepted candidates in a local queue. Claim before launch. Give Claude a task brief with stop conditions.

Use command classification as an additional check
PreToolUse hooks can return allow/ask/deny. Keep credential and destructive boundaries in enforceable rules.

Give completion checks actual evidence
Save GOAL.md with acceptance criteria. Code checks exact conditions; Jev assesses whether evidence addresses the requirement.

Calculate the decision budget
At documented rates, 600 requests per night × 4,000 tokens ≈ $3.02/month for those decisions. Track cost per accepted completed task.

Keep the state focused and the result recoverable
Compute exact values in code. Store one compact record per decision. Start with the local filter, then connect one evaluated route to a bounded worker.

Save this so you don't lose it
Follow @beamnxw for more alpha :)

Your Claude loops can burn money while nothing changes.

Empty queue. Unchanged issue. Same check, same tokens, every night.

Put those decisions on their own path and you control what starts a run.

> code gate — empty / unchanged / already claimed → skip, no model call
> Jev filter — classify the issue, check for steps + failure + expected behavior
> Opus worker — only eligible bugs get reproduced, fixed, and checked

At documented rates, hundreds of routing calls a night land around a few dollars a month. The bill that matters is cost per accepted completed task — including the mistakes.

The prompt is not the product. The gate is.

Anthropic put Opus 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 on the same 3D build task, and the benchmark gap turned out to measure the wrong thing entirely.

Both models produced geometry that passed. Passing is where the similarity ended.

> BRIEF - one identical object description handed to both models, cold
> BUILD - each one produces parts, joints and materials with no further prompting
> OPEN - every output loaded in real software instead of being scored on paper
> BEND - the models pushed until something deforms wrong or a pivot fails
> PRICE - the cost of each run set against how much human cleanup it needed

Haiku 5.5 is the cheaper model by a wide margin, and on a benchmark score the gap looks small.

The gap appears after the file opens. Geometry that scores well can still arrive with pivots in places nothing bends.

Opus 5.5 holds the constraints Haiku drops. Clearances, wall thickness, parts that have to stay separate to move.

That is the number nobody publishes. A cheap run plus two hours of cleanup is not a cheap run.

Benchmarks measure the output. The thing worth measuring is what the output costs you after it exists.

Every failure the benchmark missed and the real cost per usable model sit in the breakdown below.

Anthropic's biology model reads a sequence and tells you which organism it came from, even when nothing like it has ever been catalogued.

It has no database to match against. The answer comes out of how the sequence is written, not what it codes for.

> READ - the raw sequence taken with no species label and no known relatives
> STYLE - the usage patterns extracted, the quiet preferences every genome has
> PLACE - those patterns compared against the habits of known lineages
> GAP - anything that fits no lineage flagged rather than forced into one
> CALL - the closest branch named, with how confident the placement actually is

Every organism writes the same instructions differently. Same protein, different wording, and the wording is inherited.

That wording survives when the content does not. Two unrelated genes from one genome share a dialect.

It is the part sequencing pipelines throw away as noise before analysis even starts.

Most of what gets sequenced from soil or water belongs to nothing on record. Those reads usually get discarded.

Here they get placed. Not identified, but located, which is the first step toward being worth studying at all.

The dialect features and how the placements held up sit in the breakdown below.

The resulting map is a useful teaching tool and an example of exactly the sort of slow, low-priority work which scientists never quite get around to, but which AI now makes feasible.

Read more: https://www.anthropic.com/research/the-missing-map-of-the-sky

outsiders.text:
An astrophysicist worked with Claude Science to create the first complete ultraviolet map of the sky. Astronomers have already created complete sky maps from radio to gamma rays. But large regions of the sky have never been observed in UV.

In today’s science blog, Brice Ménard explains how he guided Claude to find existing datasets, combine them, and fill in the gaps with statistical inference. The work would have taken humans weeks of work, but, with Claude, just took a few days while Ménard worked on other projects.

The resulting map is a useful teaching tool and an example of exactly the sort of slow, low-priority work which scientists never quite get around to, but which AI now makes feasible.

Read more: https://www.anthropic.com/research/the-missing-map-of-the-sky
